I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette:
Caleb is a 25-year-old single man of North American background who works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in his city. He presented for psychological assessment reporting a cluster of distressing symptoms that, as he described them in the intake session, had been quietly dismantling his life for years before finally becoming impossible to manage.

Caleb grew up in a household where his primary caregiver - a man he describes with a flat, careful voice - would come into his room at night. The room would already be dark. Caleb remembers the particular texture of the worn cotton bedsheet pulled up to his chin, the fabric rough and pilled against his knuckles, and the sound that would sometimes precede or follow these intrusions: a younger sibling crying in the next room, audible through the thin wall. The abuse was physical and repeated across several years of his childhood. By the time it ended - through circumstance rather than any intervention - Caleb had learned to associate darkness, that specific tactile roughness, and the sound of children crying with the particular quality of helplessness and exposure he had felt as a boy.

In the years that followed, Caleb managed well enough on the surface. He finished school, found work, maintained a modest independence. But in his early twenties the symptoms intensified in ways he could no longer explain away. At night, waking in the dark of his apartment, he would find himself not merely startled but somewhere else entirely - heart hammering, skin crawling, the room feeling not like his room but like that childhood bedroom. These were not dreams he could shake off. His memories of the abuse return to him like a film that plays without his consent, and when they come, they come in full - the smell, the weight, the texture of that sheet - so completely real across his senses that stopping whatever he is doing becomes the only option. He has learned that trying to push through the memory only makes the overwhelm worse, so he stops, waits, breathes, and tries to return.

At work, the triggers find him in unexpected places. Changing bed linens - the central task of his job - means handling sheets of varying textures, and certain fabrics, rougher or more worn, produce an immediate and violent physical reaction: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and on several occasions he has had to leave a guest room abruptly and stand in the corridor until the sensation passes. He has begun requesting assignments to public spaces - lobbies, hallways - rather than guest rooms, telling his supervisor only that he is having some health issues. The consequence has been a quiet demotion in practice if not in title, and a growing awareness among his colleagues that something is off. When children are staying at the hotel and he can hear them crying in the corridors, he has found himself frozen at the housekeeping cart, unable to move.

Caleb has come to believe, with a certainty that feels unshakeable, that other people can read what happened to him simply by looking at him - that his history is somehow visible, written into his face or his posture. He feels, in moments he finds difficult to articulate, less like a person than like something acted upon, something without interior life. He is certain that harm can come from anyone, that there is no reliable way to identify who is safe, and so he has arranged his life accordingly: he makes sure never to be alone with another person if he can avoid it, always positioning himself near exits or in shared spaces. When the weight of daily demands becomes too much - the triggers at work, the nights - he finds himself drifting, retreating into an internal world where nothing can reach him. Over the past year he has let several responsibilities lapse, including a community college enrollment he had been proud of.

What finally brought Caleb to seek help was a night last month when he woke in the dark and, for several minutes, genuinely could not locate himself in time. He was most afraid, he said quietly at the end of the intake, that this was simply who he was now. What he hoped, with some difficulty, was that it didn't have to be.
